fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church 464-469, esp. 467
fields.note: The Catechism says: "We confess that one and the same Christ, Lord, and only-begotten Son, is to be acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division or separation" (CCC 467, quoting Chalcedon).

sources.label: International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article III
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says: "The Word, that is, the Son of God, did assume the human nature in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, so that there are two natures, the divine and the human, inseparably enjoined in one Person, one Christ, true God and true man, who was born of the Virgin Mary."

sources.label: International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith
National Association of Evangelicals, Statement of Faith

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 1
fields.note: The Formula of Concord says: "the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged are the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone."

fields.citation: Smalcald Articles (1537), Part II, Article 4, "Of the Papacy"
fields.note: The Smalcald Articles say: "The Pope is not, according to divine law or according to the Word of God, the head of all Christendom... but is only the bishop and pastor of the Church at Rome, and of those who voluntarily have attached themselves to him." The same article elsewhere calls the papacy "the very Antichrist" — sharper than this position's framing — while still addressing Rome as a church whose bishop and adherents are engaged as Christians in serious error rather than as no church at all.

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1213-1215, 1250
fields.note: The Catechism says: "Holy Baptism is the basis of the whole Christian life... Through Baptism we are freed from sin and reborn as sons of God" (1213), and of infants: "Born with a fallen human nature and tainted by original sin, children also have need of the new birth in Baptism" (1250).

reason: Augsburg Confession Article XIV is about the call to public ministry ("no one should publicly teach in the Church or administer the Sacraments unless he be regularly called"), not congregational membership or how belonging is constituted. No article of the Augsburg Confession addresses parish/sacramental standing as a membership category distinct from the church's general definition (Article VII), so this citation does not support the claim.

fields.citation: First Vatican Council, Dei Filius, ch. 3 (1870)
fields.note: Dei Filius says: "it was God's will that there should be linked to the internal assistance of the Holy Spirit external indications of his revelation, that is to say divine acts, and first and foremost miracles and prophecies... which are the most certain signs of revelation."

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2276-2279
fields.note: The Catechism says: "Discontinuing medical procedures that are burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary, or disproportionate to the expected outcome can be legitimate... Here one does not will to cause death" (2278), while "the ordinary care owed to a sick person cannot be legitimately interrupted" (2279).

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1883-1885, 1897-1904
fields.note: The Catechism says: "a community of a higher order should not interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, depriving the latter of its functions, but rather should support it in case of need... always with a view to the common good" (1883).

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1174-1178
fields.note: The Catechism says the Liturgy of the Hours is "so devised that the whole course of the day and night is made holy by the praise of God," in which "the faithful (clergy, religious, and lay people) exercise the royal priesthood of the baptized" (1174).

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession (1530), Article 1 (De Deo)
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says: "there is one Divine Essence which is called and which is God... and yet there are three Persons, of the same essence and power, who also are coeternal, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost."

sources.label: National Association of Evangelicals, Statement of Faith

fields.citation: Fourth Lateran Council (1215), ch. 1; First Vatican Council, Dei Filius 1; Catechism of the Catholic Church 212-213
fields.note: Lateran IV says: "there is only one true God, eternal and immense, omnipotent, unchangeable... three Persons indeed but one essence, substance, or nature absolutely simple." The Catechism adds that God "remains ever faithful to himself and to his promises" (212).

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article XI
fields.note: The Formula says election is grounded "before we had done anything good, but also before we were born, yea, even before the foundations of the world were laid, He elected us in Christ," and rejects the view "that also in us there is a cause of God's election" (Solid Declaration XI, para. 88), while treating reprobation as a mystery it declines to fold into the same account.

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2003
fields.note: The Catechism says: "There are furthermore special graces, also called charisms... Whatever their character — sometimes it is extraordinary, such as the gift of miracles or of tongues... charisms are oriented toward sanctifying grace and are intended for the common good of the Church."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article II
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says: "since the fall of Adam all men begotten in the natural way are born with sin... this disease, or vice of origin, is truly sin, even now condemning and bringing eternal death upon those not born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost."

fields.citation: Council of Vienne, 1312; Catechism of the Catholic Church 362-368
fields.note: The Council of Vienne declared that anyone who denies that the rational or intellectual soul is essentially and of itself the form of the human body is a heretic; the Catechism adds that "'soul' signifies the spiritual principle in man" (363), naming one immaterial aspect rather than two separate constitutive parts.

sources.label: Summa Theologiae
sources.citation: Thomas Aquinas, I q.75-76, on the unity of the soul

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1038
fields.note: The Catechism says: "The resurrection of all the dead, 'of both the just and the unjust,' will precede the Last Judgment... Then Christ will come 'in his glory, and all the angels with him.'"

reason: Luther's Small Catechism's explanation of the Third Article covers the Spirit's calling and sanctifying work, the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection on the Last Day; it says nothing about the soul's state or conscious presence with Christ between death and resurrection, so it does not support this citation.

fields.citation: Lumen Gentium 16 (1964); Catechism of the Catholic Church, 847
fields.note: The Catechism says: "Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart, and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience — those too may achieve eternal salvation" (847).

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article 4; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article III
fields.note: The Formula says: "our righteousness before God is [this]... that God forgives us our sins out of pure grace... that He presents and imputes to us the righteousness of Christ's obedience, on account of which righteousness we are received into grace by God, and regarded as righteous" (Solid Declaration III); the Augsburg Confession adds that faith, not works, "God imputes for righteousness in His sight" (Article 4).

fields.citation: Council of Trent, Session IV, Decree on Sacred Books (1546)
fields.note: The decree says: "if any one receive not, as sacred and canonical, these same books entire with all their parts, as they have been used to be read in the Catholic Church, and as they are contained in the old Latin vulgate edition... let him be anathema."

sources.label: Council of Trent
sources.citation: Session IV, Decree on Sacred Books (1546)

reason: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 1 states only that Scripture alone is the binding rule and norm of doctrine; it says nothing about grammatical-historical interpretation as against allegorical or typological reading. The same citation is already used, correctly, for church-history-and-authority.authority's sola-scriptura entry — reusing it here for a hermeneutic-method claim is unsupported.

fields.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1673
fields.note: The Catechism says: "The solemn exorcism, called 'a major exorcism,' can be performed only by a priest and with the permission of the bishop. The priest must proceed with prudence, strictly observing the rules established by the Church."
